title: When honoring is hard
hook: many rabbis teach that honor doesn't require accepting harm; distance can be necessary
tomorrow: hands on a kid's head every Friday night. what's being said?

segments.voice: Yesterday, kibbud av va'em: care with your hands, reverence in your words, both parents, both ways. Honor them. Today, the harder question underneath it.

Some family dinners are the kind people post. Some are the kind people brace for in the car on the way over. The Talmud praises a man named Dama ben Netina, whose mother struck him in front of others, and who didn't shame her back. So does honoring a parent mean taking whatever they hand out? Two great teachers of Jewish law looked at the hardest case and gave different answers.
screen: `THE DINNERS PEOPLE BRACE FOR.` → `DAMA DIDN'T SHAME HER BACK.` → `TAKE WHATEVER THEY HAND OUT?`

segments.voice: The case is painful. A parent's mind has become so ill that the child can't care for them without coming apart. Maimonides, in his code of law, says: honor them as far as their state allows. But if the child can't bear it, he may leave and go, and arrange for others to care for the parent properly. His best case: honor is about the parent being cared for, not about the child being destroyed. Care can be given by other hands, chosen with love. The Raavad, Rabbi Abraham ben David, writes a short, sharp note beside it: this is not right. If he leaves, whom will he leave to watch over him? His best case: nobody hired watches a parent the way a child does, and the hardest people to care for are the ones most easily abandoned. Neither says the parent stops mattering. They disagree about whose hands the care must pass through. Some rabbis today apply Maimonides' ruling to children whose parents harm them: distance can keep everyone safer, and honor can travel through others, or simply through not shaming them. One thing nobody here argues about: if you're in danger at home, reaching out is right. Call local emergency help, and in the US you can call or text 988.
screen: `MAIMONIDES: YOU MAY GO, AND ARRANGE CARE.` · `THE RAAVAD: WHO WILL WATCH HIM THEN?` · `BOTH KEEP THE PARENT IN VIEW.` · `IN DANGER? REACH OUT. 988 IN THE US.` · then, large: `HONOR WITH BOUNDARIES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one relationship that's hard to honor. In one word, name what you'd wish for it. Name what gets in the way. Then name one small plan that keeps you safe and still keeps some honor: a shorter visit, a kind text instead of a call, another person in the room.
screen: `A WISH, IN ONE WORD.` · `WHAT GETS IN THE WAY.` · `ONE SMALL, SAFE PLAN.`

segments.voice: When honoring is hard: the tradition argues it out, and both sides keep the parent in view. Distance can be part of care.
Your line: honor with boundaries. Care can travel through other hands. Day four, held gently.

howItsDone: When honoring a parent is very hard, people can ask a rabbi or a counselor for guidance; Maimonides' ruling (Laws of Rebels 6:10) is a key passage in that conversation, and safety comes first.

chat.says: lily's dad says awful stuff when he drinks. she's skipping his birthday and feels like a bad daughter. is she?
options: Not by itself. Some rabbis teach honor can keep a distance; staying safe and not shaming him counts.
Probably. Honor means showing up no matter what; Dama ben Netina took it without a word.
No, and she owes him nothing now. Honor simply ends once a parent turns cruel.
chat.meaning: Maimonides lets a child who can't bear it step away and arrange care; the parent still matters. Honor isn't the same as accepting harm.

Maimonides.meaning: Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, author of a great code of Jewish law

Raavad.meaning: Rabbi Abraham ben David, a sharp critic of Maimonides' code

Dama ben Netina.meaning: a man the Talmud praises for honoring his mother

Talmud.meaning: the great collection of rabbinic law and discussion

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Rebels (Mamrim) 6:10, with the Raavad's gloss
